content:
Psalms Chapter 112 1Hallelujah!
How blessed people are that respect the LORD
and delight in what he calls on them to do.
2 Their descendants will be successful and a blessing to their own generation.
3 They’ll have wealth and riches in their homes,
and their goodness will last forever.
4 Godly people have light in the dark;
they’re gracious, merciful, and good.
5 Goodness comes to those who graciously lend
and conduct their affairs with justice.
6 Misfortune won’t overcome them,
and people will remember the good they’ve done. Ps 112:1-6
7 Bad news doesn’t scare people like that
because they’ve committed themselves to the LORD they trust;
8they’re confident and courageous
and face their adversaries with assurance.
9 They give freely to the poor,
so their goodness lasts forever [2 Cor 9:9]
in ongoing influence and honor.
10 Sinners will see that and get mad;
they’ll grit their teeth—and leave;
what they wanted won’t happen. Ps 112:7-10

Psalms Chapter 115 1 Not to us, LORD, not to us,
but to you be honor
because of your enduring love and faithfulness.
2 Why should the nations say,
“Where’s their God?”
3 Our God is in heaven,
where he accomplishes what he intends.
4 Their man-made idols are just silver and gold
5with mouths that can’t talk,
eyes that can’t see,
6ears that can’t hear,
noses that can’t smell,
7hands that can’t feel,
feet that can’t walk,
throats that can’t make a sound!
8 The ones that make them will become like them,
likewise everybody that relies on them. Ps 115:1-8
9 Israel, trust in the LORD;
he’s your helper and shield.
10 House of Aaron, trust in the LORD;
he’s your helper and shield.
11 All of you that respect the LORD, trust in him;
he’s your helper and shield.
12 He cares about you; he’ll bless you;
Israel and Aaron;
13he’ll bless everyone that respects him,
least and greatest.
14 May he increase you and your children;
15may the Maker of earth and sky bless you. Ps 115:9-15
16 The sky belongs to him,
but he’s given us the earth.
17 The dead don’t praise the LORD;
nobody does that descends into silence;
18 but we’ll bless him
from now on forever.
Hallelujah! Ps 115:16-18

Psalms Chapter 116 1 I love the LORD because he listens to my petitions;
2so I’ll call on him as long as I live.
3 The snares of death were all around me;
the pains of Sheol came on me;
I suffered distress and sorrow.
4 Then I called on the LORD,
“Please save me.” Ps 116:1-4
5 You’re gracious and good, merciful God.
6 You preserve the simple;
when I was brought low, you saved me.
7 I can rest again
because you’ve been good to me;
8you’ve saved me from death,
my eyes from tears, my feet from stumbling.
9 I’ll walk with you in the land of the living.
10 I kept believing even when I said [2 Cor 4:13],
“I’m greatly oppressed.”
11 I said in my anxiety,
“Everybody’s lying to me!” Ps 116:5-11
12 How can I repay you, LORD,
for all your benefits?
13 I’ll lift up the cup of salvation
and call on you.
14 I’ll fulfill my vows to you
in the presence of your people.
15 You care about your holy people when they die.
16 LORD, I’m your servant,
the son of your maidservant;
you’ve removed my shackles.
17 I’ll offer you a thanksgiving sacrifice
and call on you. Ps 116:12-17
18 I’ll fulfill my vows to you
in the presence of your people,
19in the courts of your Temple in Jerusalem.
Hallelujah! Ps 116:18-19

and prosperity in your palaces.”
8 For the sake of my brothers and friends,
I say, “Peace be in you.”
9 For the sake of the Temple of the LORD our God,
I’ll seek the best for you. Ps 122:1-9

content:
Psalms Chapter 132 A Song of Ascents
1 LORD, remember David and what he suffered;
2 how he swore to the LORD
and vowed to the Mighty One of Jacob:
3 “I won’t go to my own house
or get on my bed 4 and sleep
5 till I find a place for the LORD to live,
a place for the Mighty One of Jacob.” Ps 132:1-5
6 We heard it in Ephrathah
and found it in the fields of Jaar,
7 “Let’s go to his Temple
and worship at his footstool.”
8 Come to your resting place, LORD,
you and the ark that represents your strength.
9 May your priests be arrayed in goodness,
and your holy people sing for joy.
10 For the sake of David your servant,
don’t turn away from your anointed one.
11 You’ve sworn to him
a truth you won’t take back:
“I’ll set on your throne a son from your own body [Acts 2:30].
12If your descendants keep my covenant
and the Testimony I teach them,
their descendants will also sit on your throne permanently.” Ps 132:6-12
13 You’ve chosen Zion;
you wanted to live there:
14“This is my permanent resting place;
I’ll live here because I’ve wanted it.
15I’ll abundantly bless what it can provide
and satisfy its needy ones with food.
16I’ll dress its priests in deliverance;
its holy people will sing for joy.
17I’ll make a horn from David spring up there
and light a lamp for my anointed one.
18I’ll dress his enemies in humiliation
but make his crown shine.” Ps 132:13-18

content:
Psalms Chapter 135 1Hallelujah!
Praise the LORD;
praise him, his servant,
2you that stand in his Temple,
in the courts of our God!
3 Praise him because he’s good;
sing his praises because he’s gracious,
4because he’s chosen Jacob for himself,
Israel for his own possession. Ps 135:1-4
5 I know the LORD is great,
that he’s above all gods.
6 He does what he wants
in the sky, on earth, in the seas and all their depths.
7 He makes clouds come up from the horizon;
he sends lightning with the rain
and brings the wind out of his storehouses. Ps 135:5-7
8 He struck Egypt’s firstborn,
people and animals.
9 He performed signs and wonders on Pharaoh and his people.
10 He struck many nations and slew powerful kings:
11Sihon, king of the Amorites;
Og, king of Bashan;
as well as the kingdoms in Canaan.
12 He gave their land as an inheritance
to his people Israel.
13 His name lasts forever;
his renown endures throughout all generations. 14 The LORD will vindicate his people [Heb 10:30b] and have mercy on his servants.
Ps 135:8-14
15The hand-crafted idols the nations have are just silver and gold
16with mouths that can’t talk,
with eyes that can’t see,
17with ears that can’t hear;
and they can’t breathe.
18 The ones that make them are just like them,
everybody that trusts in them too. Ps 135:15-18
19 House of Israel, bless the LORD;
House of Aaron, bless the LORD; 20 House of Levi, bless the LORD;
you that respect the LORD, bless him.
21 From Zion bless the LORD,
who lives in Jerusalem.
Hallelujah! Ps 135:19-21

His love is everlasting. 2 Give thanks to the God of gods.
His love is everlasting. 3 Give thanks to the Lord of lords,
His love is everlasting. 4 to him alone that does great things,

His love is everlasting; 15 but overthrew Pharaoh and his army in it;
His love is everlasting; Ps 136:10-15

His love is everlasting; 18 and slew them:

His love is everlasting. Ps 136:16-22
23who remembered us in our low estate

His love is everlasting. Ps 136:23-26

content:
Psalms Chapter 137 1 We sat by the rivers in Babylon
and cried when we remembered Zion.
2 We hung our harps on its willows.
3 Our captors required us to sing there;
our tormentors demanded happy songs, “Sing us a song from Zion.” Ps 137:1-3
4 How can we sing about the LORD in a foreign land?
5 If I forget you, Jerusalem,
may my right hand wither.
6 May my tongue stick to the roof of my mouth
if I don’t remember you,
if I don’t regard Jerusalem above my greatest joy.
7 Remember, LORD, against the Edomites
the day of Jerusalem, when they said to the Babylonians,
“Tear it down, tear it down to its foundation.”
8 Young woman of Babylon, you devastated one,
how happy will be the one that repays you
with what you did to us.
9 How happy will the one be that grabs your infants
and dashes them against the rocks! Ps 137:4-9

Psalms Chapter 138 A Psalm of David
1 I thank you with all my heart
and sing your praises in front of the mighty.
2 I bow toward your holy Temple
and thank you for your enduring love and faithfulness,
because you’ve guaranteed your promises with the honor your name has.
3 You answered me when I called out to you
and made me bold with strength. Ps 138:1-3
4 Kings will thank you, LORD,
when they hear what you say.
5 They’ll sing about your ways
because your honor is so great.
6 Though you’re high above us,
you care about the lowly;
but you recognize the proud from a long way off.
7 Though I’m in trouble, you’ll protect me
and reach out against my enemies to save me.
8 You’ll accomplish the purposes you have for me;
your love endures forever, LORD.
Don’t abandon the ones you’ve created. Ps 138:4-8

content:
Psalms Chapter 139 For the Choir Director. A Psalm of David
1 LORD, you’ve known me and examined me.
2 You know when I sit down and when I get up;
from a long way off you know what I’m thinking.
3 You search out my traveling and my resting;
you’re well acquainted with my ways.
4 Before I speak,
you know what I’m going to say.
5 You’ve protected me front and back
and laid your hand over me.
6 Knowledge like that is too amazing for me;
it’s beyond me; I can’t imagine it. Ps 139:1-6
7 Where can I go from your Spirit?
Where can I go to get away from you?
8 If I go up to the sky, you’re there;
if I make my bed in Sheol, you’re there.
9 If I take the wings of morning
and live by the most distant part of the ocean,
10 even there you’ll lead me and support me.
11 If I say, “Let darkness cover me,
and the light around me become night,”
12the dark’s not dark to you;
the night’s as bright as day.
Ps 139:7-12
13 You formed my inner parts
and knit me together in my mother’s womb.
14 Thank you; the way you’ve made me is awesome and wonderful.
What you do is marvelous;
I know that for sure. 15 My frame wasn’t hidden from you
when I was being made in secret,
intricately put together deep in the earth.
16 You saw my unshaped substance;
you wrote in your scroll
the length of life you appointed for me
before there was any of it. Ps 139:13-16
17 How precious your thoughts are to me!
How vast their number is!
18 If I could count them, they’d outnumber the grains of sand.
When I wake up, I’m still with you.

(Go away from me, you murderers!)
20 Your enemies say awful things about you;
they use your name as a byword. 21 Don’t I hate those who hate you?
Don’t I despise the ones that oppose you?
22 I have total disdain for them;
they’re my enemies.
23 Examine me, God, and know my heart;
test me and see how anxious my thoughts are.
24 See if there’s anything offensive in me
and lead me in the everlasting way. Ps 139:17-24
title: Psalms 139

content:

content:
Psalms Chapter 140 For the Choir Director. A Psalm of David
1 LORD, rescue me from sinful people
protect me from violent men,
2that plot evil things in their minds,
and constantly stir up conflict.
3 They have pointed tongues like snakes;
vipers’ venom lies behind their lips [Rom 3:13b]. 4 LORD, protect me from sinful people;
protect me from violent men, that try to trip me.
5 The arrogant hide traps for me;
with cords they spread a net beside the road
and set snares for me. Ps 140:1-5 6 I said to the LORD, “You’re my God;
listen to my petitions.
7 GOD the Lord, my strong deliverer,
you’ve protected my head in battle.
8 Don’t let sinful people do whatever they please;
don’t further their evil intentions. 9 “Make the schemes they talk about come down on their own heads.
10 Let burning coals fall on them;
throw them into the fire,
into deep pits they can’t climb out of.
11 Don’t let slanderers get a foothold in the earth;
have misfortune hunt down violent people quickly.”
12 I know you’ll champion the cause of the suffering
and render justice for the poor.
13 The godly will thank you
and live in your presence. Ps 140:6-13

content:
Psalms Chapter 141 A Psalm of David
1 LORD, I’m calling on you; come quick;
hear me out.
2 Consider my prayer as incense and the raising of my hands as an evening offering.
3 Guard my mouth;
watch over my lips.
4 Incline my heart away from anything evil,
from practicing sinful things with sinners. Ps 141:1-4
5 Let a godly person strike me or rebuke me graciously;
that would be ointment for my head;
Don’t let me refuse it.
I still pray constantly against the deeds of sinners.
6 When their leaders are thrown over the cliffs;
they’ll learn that the LORD’s word is true.
7 “Like someone plowing up rocks,
our bones have been scattered at the mouth of Sheol.”
8 I look to you, Lord GOD,
and take refuge in you; don’t leave me with no defense. 9 Keep me from the jaws of the trap they’ve set for me,
from sinners’ snares;
10may they stumble into their own nets
while I go on by safely. Ps 141:5-10

content:
Psalms Chapter 142 A Maskil of David when he was in the cave
A Prayer
1 I cry out to the LORD
and petition him;
2I pour out my complaint to him
and tell him my troubles.
3 When I feel overwhelmed, he knows the route I should take;
they’ve hidden traps for me
on every path I walk.
4 I look in every direction,
but nobody notices me.
There’s no escape for me;
nobody cares if I live. Ps 142:1-4
5 I’m calling out to you, LORD;
“You’re my refuge,
my portion among the living.
6Listen to my outcry
because I’m in desperate need;
deliver me from my persecutors;
they’re just too strong.
7Bring me out of prison
so I can thank you;
the godly gather around me
because you’ve been so good to me.” Ps 142:5-7

content:
Psalms Chapter 143 A Psalm of David
1 Hear my prayer, LORD;
listen to my petition;
in your faithfulness and goodness, come to my relief.
2 Don’t put me on trial
because, compared to you, nobody’s good.
3 My enemy has chased me,
crushed me on the ground,
and made me sit in the dark like people long dead.
4 So I feel overwhelmed,
and my heart is empty.
5 I remember the old days; I ponder everything you’ve done
and think about what you’ve made.
6 I reach out for you,
thirsty for you like parched ground. Ps 143:1-6
7 Answer me right away, LORD; my spirit is failing; don’t hide from me,
or I’ll get like those destined for the Pit.
8 Let me hear about your enduring love every morning
because I put my trust in you;
show me where to walk
because I’m lifting myself up to you.
9 Deliver me from my enemies;
you’re my refuge.
10 Teach me how to do your will
because you’re my God;
let your good Spirit lead me on level ground.
11 In defense of your honor, LORD, protect me;
in your goodness, take me away from trouble;
12 in your enduring love, slay my enemies;
destroy the ones that abuse me,
because I’m your servant. Ps 143:7-12

content:
Psalms Chapter 144 A Psalm of David
1 Bless the LORD, my Rock,
who trains my hands for war,
my fingers for battle.
2 He’s my enduring love and fortress,
my stronghold and deliverer,
my shield and refuge,
who subdues nations.
3 LORD, what are we that you give us any thought
or care about us?
4 We’re like a breath;
our lifetime is like a passing shadow. Ps 144:1-4
5 Lower the sky, LORD, and come down;
touch the mountains and make them smoke.
6 Throw your lightning bolts and scatter my enemies;
shoot your arrows and rout them.
7 Reach down from on high
and rescue me from deep water,
from aliens 8 that lie,
whose right hand deceives.
9 I’ll sing you a new song, God;
I’ll sing praise to you on a ten-string harp.
10 You deliver kings
and rescued David from the cruel sword.
11 Deliver me from aliens that lie,
whose right hand deceives. Ps 144:5-11
12 Make our sons in their youth like grown-up plants
and our daughters like corner pillars in a palace.
13 Fill our granaries with every kind of crop;
have our flocks bear thousands—tens of thousands—in our pastures.
14 Have our cattle deliver without miscarriage or failure to bear;
make it so there’s no danger in our streets.
15 How happy people are that have such blessings;
how blessed they are that have the LORD as their God! Ps 144:12-15

content:
Psalms Chapter 145 A Psalm of Praise. by David
1 I’ll praise you highly, my God and king,
and bless you forever.
2 I’ll bless you every day
and praise you from now on.
3 You’re great and deserve great praise;
you have a greatness we have no way to measure.
4 One generation will praise your works to the next
and tell about the powerful things you’ve done.
5 They’ll think about your majestic glory and splendor
and about your amazing acts.
6 People will talk about the power evident in your awesome deeds
and tell how great you are.
7 They’ll overflow with the fame of your abundant goodness
and loudly sing about your godliness. Ps 145:1-7
8 The LORD is gracious and merciful,
slow to get angry and great in enduring love.
9 He’s good to everyone;
his mercy spreads out across his whole creation.
10 Everything he’s made will thank him;
his holy people will bless him.
11 They’ll speak of the honor his kingdom has
and talk about his power
12to make known his powerful deeds
and the glorious majesty of his kingdom.
13 His kingdom lasts forever;
his dominion continues across all generations. Ps 145:8-13
14 The LORD catches the ones that fall down
and straightens up those who are bent over.
15 Everyone looks to him for help,
and he gives them their food as needed.
16 He meets the needs of every living thing.
17 The LORD shows his goodness in everything he does,
his kindness in every deed.
18 He’s near to those who call on him,
that call on him sincerely.
19 He provides for the people who respect him;
he hears their call and saves them.
20 He protects those who love him,
but destroys the sinful.
21 I’ll speak praise to the LORD;
everyone will bless him forever. Ps 145:14-21

content:
Psalms Chapter 146 1 Praise the LORD, my soul!
2 I’ll praise my God as long as I live
and sing praises to him as long as I’m here.
3 Don’t rely on rulers,
mortals, who can’t help.
4 They quit breathing and go back into the ground;
their plans come to an end at the same time.
5 How blessed they are that have Jacob’s God to help them,
whose hope lies in the LORD
6 that made earth and sky,
the ocean and everything in them,
that’s dependable forever,
7 who renders justice to the oppressed,
who feeds the hungry
and sets the prisoners free. Ps 146:1-7
8 He gives sight to the blind,
lifts up the burdened,
and loves the godly. 9 He protects foreigners
and supports widows and the fatherless,
but thwarts the sinful.
10 The LORD will reign forever,
your God, Zion, to all generations.
Hallelujah!
Ps 146:8-10

title: Psalms 146

content:
Psalms Chapter 147 1Hallelujah!
It’s good to sing praises to our God;
praising him is fitting because he’s gracious.
2 The LORD builds up Jerusalem
and gathers the outcasts in Israel.
3 He heals the brokenhearted
and bandages up their wounds.
4 He counts the stars and calls them each by name.
5 Our Lord is great and has great power,
and understanding without limit.
6 He supports the abused
and takes sinners down to the ground. Ps 147:1-6
7 Sing thanksgiving to the LORD;
sing praise to our God with a lyre.
8 He covers the sky with clouds,
provides rain for the ground,
and makes grass grow on the hills.
9 He gives animals their food
and feeds the young ravens when they caw.
10 He doesn’t delight in the strength of horses or take pleasure in human might.
11 The LORD favors those who respect him,
who place their hopes in his enduring love. Ps 147:7-11
12 Praise the LORD, Jerusalem;
praise your God, Zion.
13 He’s reinforced the bars on your gates
and blessed those who reside in you.
14 He brings peace to your borders
and satisfies you with the finest wheat.
15 He issues his command to the world,
and his message travels swiftly.
16 He sends snow like wool
and scatters frost like ashes.
17 He makes it hail;
who can stand his freezing cold?
18 He speaks and it melts;
he makes wind blow and water flow.
19 He declares his message to Jacob,
his statutes and ordinances to Israel.
20 He hasn’t dealt this way with any other nation;
they haven’t known his ordinances.
Hallelujah! Ps 147:12-20

Psalms Chapter 148 1Hallelujah! Praise the LORD from heaven;
praise him in the sky.
2 Praise him, all his hosts of angels.
3 Praise him, sun and moon
and shining stars.
4 Praise him, highest heaven,
and water vapor in the sky.
5 Let them praise the LORD
because he commanded and they came to be.
6He established them forever
by a decree that won’t expire. Ps 148:1-6
7 Praise the LORD from earth,
you sea monsters and all the great deep,
8fire and hail, snow and clouds,
stormy wind fulfilling his command,
9mountains and hills,
fruit trees and cedars,
10wild animals and livestock,
crawling things and flying birds,
11kings of the earth and all the nations,
officials and judges
12 young men and virgins,
old men and children.
13 Praise the LORD
because he alone is to be esteemed;
his honor towers higher than earth and sky.
14He makes his people strong
and establishes praise for his holy nation,
for Israel that’s near him. Hallelujah! Ps 148:7-14

Sing the LORD a new song;
praise him in the assembly of his holy people.
2 Be happy in your Maker, Israel;
celebrate your King, people of Zion.
3 Praise him with dancing;
sing praises with tambourines and lyres,
4because the LORD delights in you
and graces harassed people with deliverance. Ps 149:1-4

sing for joy on your couches.

and punishment on peoples,
8 to bind kings with chains
and nobles with iron restraints,
9 to carry out prescribed judgment on them.
That’s an honor for all his holy people.

CONDITION vs. CAUSE
A condition is an action required of one person by another. The other person act does not produce the result; it meets the condition for the first person to give the result. Jesus’ reference to the brazen serpent in the Old Testament illustrates idea (John 3:14-15). The Israelites were to look on the brazen serpent to be cured from snakebite. Looking at the brazen serpent did not cause the cure. God gave the cure if a person did the looking.

“Prophets who prophesied about the grace that would come to you searched out this salvation carefully. They wanted to find out what time or kind of time the Spirit of Christ in them was indicating about his sufferings and subsequent glories. They learned that they weren’t ministering these things to themselves but to you. The Holy Spirit, sent from heaven, has announced those things …
title: Connections

content:
Embarking on a new venture calls for calculating reward against risk. Risk considers possible failures and unforeseen consequences. Reward ushers in desired prospects—perhaps even better than hoped. Somehow we measure negatives before choosing to proceed.
In the case of an all-knowing, all-powerful God, laying a foundation for human salvation did not risk failure. Success was guaranteed by the character of the Son: his righteousness and his willingness even to lay his life on the line. The …
title: No Risk for Sure

content:
It’s easier to stay out of trouble than to get out of it. It’s easier to avoid a problem than to solve it. But gathering here acknowledges that the “human problem” already exists; broken relationship with God and ruined friendships between people have already become the case for all of us.
More than that, the solution to the “human problem” is also in place as this memorial to Christ’s ultimate human righteousness shows. What it took to solve that problem shows how important solving it was and …
title: Remembering the Solution

content:
“This Do in Remembrance of Me.” Jesus’ words traditionally appear on communion tables for everyone in the congregation to see. They come from his last meal with the disciples, when he instituted this memorial.
Among the many things this observance refreshes is that he never asks us to do more than he shows us he is willing to do.
So, taking these emblems today prepares us for any unforeseen challenge that may be on the way this week. That pain, that disappointment, that rejection or loss will be …
title: Let’s Remember That

content:
“Well begun, half done”; but “half done is not done.” Laying a foundation does not give us a place to live. Cutting firewood does not keep us warm. Going to the store does not feed a family. Resisting Satan’s temptations in the beginning would not have sufficed to offset caving in to them at Calvary—as in “come down from the cross.” Jesus would not have “finished” the Father’s will for his life in our realm.
In the extreme, Jesus modeled carry-through in godly living and thereby obtained for us …
title: Carrying Through

content:
Jesus was not alone in dark Gethsemane; an angel came to strengthen him (Luke 22:43). The same thing happened in the beginning of his ministry when Satan tempted him for forty days (Mark 1:13). These two episodes illustrate the power of personal presence; it can enable a person to deal even with extreme issues like near starvation and prospective agony.
Influence is not miracle. We suppose the angels came to encourage, not to give ability, not to reduce his hunger drive in the desert or increase …
title: Not Alone

content:
Work is productive doing; it stresses the intended consequence of effort. Christ’s “work” on the cross completed his sinless life. It resulted in becoming the sinless One we devote ourselves to in this observance.
So, beyond pledging allegiance, we are renewing efforts at working like him in self-sacrifice to God and the good of other people.
Christian observance does not consist of going through religious motions. The Lord’s Supper is no exception. It is doing something for effect, in this case …
title: Christ’s Final Work

content:
The emblems graphically picture what has to happen for joy to come. The pattern holds for life as a whole and for its segments. Meantime, living for him calls for effort, struggle, even suffering for there to be a “not yet” that is worth it all. The harder the labor, the more fulfilling the results. If we’re not willing to deal with the humiliation, we’re not worthy of receiving the exaltation.
In everyday work, we sometimes put out a lot of effort that does not yield the desired result. Such is …
title: His Guarantee

content:
Jesus appointed two ordinances for us to keep after he returned to the Father. Before he ascended, he included baptism in the Great Commission (Matthew 28:19) for identifying with himself, the Father, and the Spirit. Earlier, on the eve of his death, he instituted this “supper,” communion, the eucharist, as we variously term it. Both ordinances have ties to his death, the focal point and destiny of his ministry.
Among its many aspects, this ordinance carries with it an element of worship. It …
title: An Appointed Obedience

content:
A black-and-white picture lacks color. A snapshot lacks movement. Watching a party of friends on TV lacks the experience of participating. Illustrations like these lack an element that would make them better, more real, more interesting, more fulfilling.
Existing is less than living because it lacks what we call meaning. Christ came to give us life and to give it more abundantly, the sense of value that comes from friendship with our creator, the sense that he cares about us.
The bread and juice …
title: In Living Color

content:
Jesus had his disciples go with him into Gethsemane the night before his crucifixion. He took three of them deeper into the olive orchard, asking them to join him in keeping watch (Matthew 26:38). Even his threefold prayer for deliverance from the cross in nine hours appealed to the power of relationship, relationship with the Father about the approaching temptations and trials.
Luke notes that an angel appeared to him to strengthen him (24:43). The text does not suggest that the angels on the …
title: The Power of Personal Presence

content:
The records of what happened in Gethsemane show how hard the situation was on Jesus. Luke’s gospel even has a possible added note about his sweating drops of blood during that experience. How he managed the situation can guids us in doing likewise.
Yielding to temptation is easier than resisting it. We enjoy the experience; that’s why we do it. So we must remember that actions have consequences. If we don’t want some consequence, we have to resist the temptation that leads to it. If we want the …
title: The Joy That Overcame the Dread

content:
Ideas, words, and symbols are not real; so thinking, talking, and observing rituals do not accomplish anything in themselves. They do not ‘become” real till they become “actions.”
When we do something we experience something, and not before. A communion service is for bringing our ‘selves” into the real presence of the “Living Word” so our behaviors become impacted.
Realizing such a simple point can prompt us to choose to do, and so to experience, the difference that being with Christ makes in …
title: Beyond Words

content:
When we do something, we say something; when we do something, we teach something. Breaking bread together “proclaims Christ’s death till he returns” (1 Corinthians 11:26). Paul notes what happened and what it meant.
His comment also splices calvary and Christ’s return. We keep that point in mind during this “meantime” era. We reach back to grasp his death and reach forward to take hold of his return. The former, verified by his resurrection, undergirds our confidence in the latter, which …
title: A Mark of Christians

content:
Christianity has two ordinances, and they deal with the same concern: the sin problem. Both ordinances derive from the same event: Christ’s death to solve that problem. We can revisit that connection by reading Romans 6:1-13:
“So should we say, ‘Let’s keep sinning so there’ll be more grace’? 2Goodness, no! How can we who died to sin keep living in it? 3Don’t you know that we who were baptized into Christ Jesus, were baptized into his death? 4Baptism buried us with him into death. As the Father …
title: Freedom For

content:
Being locked into anything means bondage to it, something that someone else often has to free us from.
Accordingly, Paul speaks of “crucifying” the sinful body, no longer being a “slave” to sin, dying to sin and being “dead” in it (Romans 6:6, 7, 11), not being under the perfection necessity that law-keeping in theory requires.
This freedom from “slavery” to the consequences of sin comes, not from ourselves, but from the One sinned against, from the One who completed his righteousness before the …
title: Freedom From

content:
The overwhelming cost of freedom from tyranny, abuse, and persecution! Today we are probably more aware of that cost than ever before. Modern communication networks can inform us almost immediately of atrocities anywhere they happen. With each new threat, we experience anew the cost in lives, resources, and the time that it takes to undo such deplorable conditions for masses of humanity.
When it comes to freedom from the sin that lives in each of us, all the negative factors come to the fore in …
title: What Price Freedom

content:
Goodness has only to do with how persons interact with each other, with ways of behaving that affect and enable living together. (a) Goodness is person-al.
Goodness has to do only with a person’s own behavior. God does not hold my sin against my son, my friend, my fellow human being. The Law of Moses said the one who does God’s commandments is the one that has life by them (Leviticus 18:5 &lt; Galatians 3:12). The prophet said that the goodness or sinfulness of a person will be on himself …
title: How Goodness Works

content: A paraphrase of Romans 5:8 can read, “God has demonstrated his love for us in that even while we were sinners, he sent his Son to die on a cross for us.” We do not want to overlook the role of the Father’s love. Giving ourselves up is easier than feeling responsible for letting someone else suffer. Here the Father is not only “letting” but “designing” the basis for human salvation. More than that, he did it while we were still sinners. And, this all stands on top of the fact that we brought this …
title: The Father and the Crucifixion

content:
“Take the attitude that Christ Jesus took. Although he was existing in the form of deity, he did not consider it something to cling to. He emptied himself and took on the form of a servant in the likeness of a man. Being found in the form of a man, he humbled himself by becoming obedient to the point of death on a cross” (Philippians 2:5-8).
So, humility participates in the very foundation of our faith and the salvation that lies at the heart of it. Consequently, when we observe the Lord’s …
title: The Humility of God

content:
Our Father sent our Brother into our situation to live out human righteousness to its highest level: self-sacrifice. Completing that venture in our realm, qualified him as savior of human children. So, the Father appointed him as sacrifice, savior, and priest in the true tabernacle of heaven itself. Committing ourselves to him is the Father’s condition for considering us righteous like him, which is the positive side of forgiveness.
These emblems picture Christ’s body given and his blood shed. …
title: The Appointed Savior

content:
We dare not forget about the past, because it has so much to do with creating the possibilities that have arisen from it. We use various ways of connecting to crucial events that flow down to us. Besides simply remembering, we carry out rituals, we build memorials, we use emblems to bridge the gap between then and now.
We also sing songs like “Were You There When They Crucified My Lord?” The emblems are a way of putting us there, emblems Jesus himself instituted so we would continue to be …
title: A Way to Remember

content:
Christ’s tomb has a broken seal, a stone rolled aside from the entrance, and a void within. That scene serves as a visual reminder of hope no matter what. Death is the most extreme negative that we will face—and we will all face it, but the open tomb of Jesus pictures relentless hope for us as his people.
If an empty tomb can follow a deadly cross, good can follow anything. As the Lord endured the cross because of what lay beyond it, we cling to relentless hope through everything we encounter …
title: Relentless Hope

content:
During their wilderness wanderings, God gave manna to the followers of Moses to keep them physically alive in the desert. Jesus plays on that occurrence when speaking of himself as a kind of manna, or “food,” that God sent into the world to give spiritual life to his people.
Jesus calls on us to internalize what he stands for in values and purposes, to taker into our physical selves what he stood for while he lived among us. Taking his character into ourselves is like “eating” him, becoming like …
title: Lifegiving Bread (John 6:22-71)

content:
Sporting events provide a familiar picture of opposing efforts: the Olympics, the Iditarod, the World Series, March Madness, the Super Bowl, and the like. The games in all these sports share one feature: they end in victory and defeat.
Competitions like these parallel what we call attention to in this ordinance: the competition between good and evil, between God and what opposes him, between the victory and defeat that come.
The most significant point is that the story we are remembering did not …
title: Snatching Victory from Defeat

content: As many of us as look at Christ’s cross can see its connection with ourselves. That is so regardless—regardless of who we are, what we have done or failed to do. Since we are all different in failures, mistakes, and sins, we specialize the meaning of the cross to the needs distinctive to ourselves. That is so regardless of what the sins were (Matthew 12:31), how bad they were, how often we committed them, when we did them, how long we lived that way, regardless of who we sinned against and …
title: Whoever We Are

content:
These emblems do not represent an idea but an event; more particularly they are reminders of a personal event and the features that involves; “Do this in remembrance of me.”
These notations relate to comments about theory versus practice. Life in Christ is not something theoretical, something abstract or distant, something applicable to earlier times. We are people, and our needs are real and present like they have been in the past all along the way.
The person of Christ, his life and death, …
title: Something Real Here

content:
Vicious men have a strategy. They believe they can better get us to deny the faith by threatening to torture one of our loved ones in our presence. We probably would rather face such things ourselves than be “responsible” for a loved one’s agony.
Something of that point applies to Christ’s crucifixion. The Son was willing to show his love for us by enduring the cross as the way of “laying down his own life for his friends” (John 15:13). Beyond that, the Father was responsible for his Son’s going …
title: From the Father’s Viewpoint

content:
Things do not mean anything unless they are connected to other things. What we say, what we know, what we own, what we do are pointless in themselves. In 1 Corinthians 13:2-3 Paul observes that, even in their extreme forms, words, knowledge, possessions, deeds do not mean anything unless we use them in connection with caring about other people:
“If I speak in the languages of people and angels but don’t have love, like a noisy gong or crashing cymbal I don’t mean anything. If I prophesy, …
title: No Pointless Cross

content: The author of the Fourth Gospel termed himself “the disciple Jesus loved.” Presumably he wanted to keep his involvement from being too prominent and perhaps distracting while still emphasizing his personal witness of what he records. Choosing this self-designation later in life when he wrote may reflect Jesus’ influence on him from early being one of the “sons of thunder” (Mark 3:17). Instead of a contrast, however, “the disciple Jesus loved” may be an understatement that any disciple might …
title: Disciples Jesus Loved

content:
The beginning of the week is a good time to take stock, turning our minds backward, upward, inward, and forward. The Lord’s Supper touches on all these directions.
It looks backward to Christ’s giving himself in crucifixion for us. It looks upward in gratitude to the Father for grace and love of such a degree that he was willing to give up his Son for our salvation. It looks inward in self-examination that prompts sensitivity to matters of character and gratitude (1 Corinthians 11:28). It looks …
title: Spiritual Directions

content:
We consider the beginning of the year as a time to start over. Gathering at the Lord’s table relates to that same idea. Having a clean slate feels good. It gives us a sense of release from whatever went before that would hinder going forward. We are remembering here a unique event that provides us with that feeling of release from past failures that can weigh us down and sap the energy for trying again.
So drawing our minds back toward the One who loves us that much and loved us that way as a …
title: A Time to Restart

content:
The greatest gift is the gift of yourself. The most extreme example of it we are remembering here at this table: it is unforgettable.
We use the cross of Jesus as an ornament on our jewelry. The image has become an architectural feature on our buildings. It took Jesus’ self-giving to transform the ugliness of the cross into something beautiful. It took what he did to transform the dreaded cross into a welcome means of reconciliation by love for alienated people.
Observing the bread and the fruit …
title: The Greatest Gift

content:
“From a crib to a cross” indicates innocence on both ends of life, from start to finish. We needed that kind of life as a model and a basis for our own innocence.
The Christmas story is stripped of life’s distractions. The Magi came to the palace in the capital, but Jesus had entered the world eight miles south of there in a barn. Instead of finding him with the king, the Wise Men found him in a house with a carpenter and his young wife. They did not approach a powerful ruler; they knelt to a …
title: From a Crib to a Cross

content:
“Today” is a word from Jesus on the cross. He said it to one of the two insurrectionists the soldiers had crucified with him. The one he was talking to had evidently taken part in yet another attempt to overthrow Roman rule in Israel. He likely had the typical Jewish expectancy that Messiah would liberate his nation.
Earlier he joined the other criminal in taunting Jesus to bring the three of them down from their crosses. Now he has had a change of heart as death drew nearer and darkness at …
title: Today

content: We are taking part in a worldwide observance that has been going on for 2,000 years. Not only that, but Messiah’s death applies to the Mosaic era as well. The Hebrew writer says, “a death having taken place for transgressions under the first covenant” (Hebrews 9:15). But that is still not the whole story. “The gospel was preached even to the dead that were disobedient in the days of Noah” (1 Peter 3:19). Everyone’s destiny will be figured in relation to the event that we are remembering here at …
title: Everywhere All the Time

content:
Colossians 3:1 speaks of Christ seated on the right hand of God’s throne. Jesus himself pictured the path to life for us on earth as narrow, passing through the “strait” gate, a path that few seem to find. In his own case, the narrow path was also an uphill climb that led through calvary, the empty tomb through the ascension above the clouds to the right hand of the Father.
The general pattern applies to those of us who make an effort to be his followers. For some of us, the narrow, uphill path …
title: The Upward Journey

content:
Almost as an aside, Paul tells the Thessalonians “not to get weary with well doing” (2 Thessalonians 3:13). His comment strikes at an important point in our endeavors: not to quit before we’re done. Sometimes without our knowing it, success lies just ahead if we keep at it a little longer.
Jesus spent more than three years traveling, teaching, healing, resisting temptation, and being rejected. The night and morning before his last afternoon, he was up all night being arrested, deserted, …
title: Perseverance

content: In the process of receiving the Ten Commandments, Moses asked to see God’s glory. God responded, “You cannot see my face because people cannot see me and live” (Exodus 32:20). We might take the comment in two ways. Does it mean we cannot see God while we are alive, or does it warn that seeing God would kill us? Some of the ancients seem to have had this belief (Genesis 32:30; Judges 6:22-23; 13:21-22). The less extreme meaning equals Paul’s comment that in the next stage of existence we will see …
title: See God and Live

content:
Antidote to Fear
Taking this bread and fruit of the vine is like taking an antidote. The elements themselves are not the antidote; it’s what they represent that’s the antidote to condemnation. “Being justified by his blood, we’ll be saved from wrath” (Romans 5:8). John speaks similarly in a context about judgment, punishment, and the fear of it, “Perfect love casts out fear” (1 John 4:18), that is, full-grown love for God takes away foreboding about the eternal future.
What holds true for the …
title: Halloween

content:
Which was the better football team in a game that went 21 to 20? Which team was better in a game that went 76 to 2? The second game offers a clearer case.
Seeing things in the extreme makes them clearer and more certain. That God cares about us may not seem clear in a situation where people dislike us, where natural disasters overwhelm us, where health issues weigh us down, where the future looks bleak.
That Christianity is true may not seem clear when we are pressed by alternative beliefs about …
title: In the Extreme

content:
Old Testament events admonish us with their implications. The account about Jonah the prophet is a case in point. When he preached to the people in Nineveh, they believed him and acted on his warning by fasting, putting on sackcloth, and sitting in ashes. Their stricken conscience responded to Jonah’s forthright proclamation, “In forty days Nineveh will be destroyed” (Jonah 3:4). This lone foreign figure didn’t perform any miracles in their streets to confirm his claim.
We have more reason to …
title: A Call to Repentance

content:
Human resistance does not thwart divine intention. The cross represents human resistance; the empty tomb represents divine triumph. The communion we observe on Sunday testifies to the divine triumph over human resistance last Friday; otherwise, there would be no reason to observe it. In this case, that earlier rebellion even helped accomplish the divine intent.
In effect, the Jewish people and the religious leaders in Jesus’ day had tried to redefine the Messiah’s role away from personal …
title: Divine Intention

content:
Christ’s cross serves as the ultimate symbol of temptation; his empty tomb nearby is a monument to conquered temptation.
Scripture says he was tempted in all the ways we are—and more, we might add—yet without failing (Hebrews 4:15). At the start of his ministry, he was tempted while hungry, thirsty, and weak. In the end of his ministry, he was tempted with excruciating pain. All the while meantime, he faced rejection, mockery, and betrayal.
Under such intense levels of typical human challenges, …
title: Overcoming Temptation

content:
At the beginning of his ministry, Jesus made a choice that led to what we are remembering today. Satan offered him leadership over all the kingdoms of the world if he would yield to Satan’s direction over his life and work. Jesus chose not to accept that offer.
Giving him worldwide dominion would have given him the very thing Jewish people were so desperately expecting their Messiah to have. If he had agreed to that role, contemporary Israelis would have accepted him. He would not have faced the …
title: Universal Lordship

content:
Paul’s comments about communion include discernment. That means, first of all, that it not get lost inside a meal—as a course in the love feast he cautions his readers about in 1 Corinthians 11:17-22. It means not letting this observance be a pointless ritual. More personally it calls for discerning the body of Christ in it (11:29) and discerning ourselves as we participate (11:31).
Coming to the table reserves a place in our gathering for introspection. That is a natural thing to do because …
title: Discerning the Body

content:
In this observance we highlight the most important event that ever took place. The death of the Lamb of God provides a solution for the problem of sin on this side of the grave. Besides, it establishes the terms of judgment on the other side of the grave. It’s the focal point of history and the basis for eternal destinies. From this speck of space and this tick in time, we bring ourselves into God’s eternal, universal purpose.
Important issues call for extreme measures. In this case, the issue …
title: An Extreme Measure

content:
Even when we are trying to “do the right thing,” ignorance gets us into mistakes and sins that range from minor to major. The Proverbial writer noted long ago, “There’s a way that seems right, but it leads to death” (Proverbs 14:12).
Jesus’ amazing words on the cross were, “Forgive them, Father; they don’t know what they’re doing” (Luke 23:34). In the early days of the church, Peter told the Jewish crowd, “You killed the Prince of life. . . . I know you did it in ignorance as did your rulers” …
title: Saving Us from Ourselves

content:
The conclusion of one thing can become the beginning of something further. Looking back at what has happened lays the groundwork for what should come. Christ’s death to sin was not the end of the matter; it led to the end of the matter: his living to God.
Our baptism into his death is not the end of the matter either; it leads to living to God. The Lord’s Supper looks two ways at once—back to what happened and forward to what is to happen when “sin is washed away.”
It pledges us not to let “sin …
title: Romans 6:10-12a

content:
With many things, if we do not do them completely, we may as well not do them at all. Preparing the ground, planting the seed, watering the plants does not amount to anything if we don’t harvest the crop. Laying a foundation and setting up walls and rafters does not amount to anything if we don’t roof the building. We must finish what we start to get any benefit out of it.
All of Christ’s teaching and miracles, his prayers and persecution, his efforts at defending his message would not have laid …
title: Commitment to the End

content:
The cross symbolizes Christ, the Christian faith, and salvation from sin. It was the focal point of our Lord’s several acts of compassion leading up to his death.
He healed the ear of Malchus, one of those who had come to arrest him (John 18:10). He told the soldiers to let his disciples go and just arrest him (John 18:8). He told the begging insurrectionist on the cross beside him that he would be with him in Paradise that same day (Luke 23:43). He tried to warn his executioners what they were …
title: Another Lesson from the Cross

content:
The Passover lamb foreshadowed the real thing: “The Lamb of God that takes away the sin that is in the world” (John 1:29). By analogy, that Passover lamb offered on an altar was to be without blemish (Exodus 12:5) like what it foreshadowed sacrificed on a cross.
These emblems represent Christ’s final demonstration of unblemished righteousness that laid the foundation for our righteousness. His life’s consummation on the cross epitomized his whole life of righteousness. We are remembering here …
title: The Passover Lamb

content:
These emblems not only remind us; they teach us. Hebrews 12:2 recommends “looking to Jesus the author and perfecter of faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, disregarded the shame, and sat down on the right hand of God’s throne.” The glory beyond the agony became an aid to enduring it.
Christ has engendered trust in him (author) and carried trust to its highest demonstration in the way he died (perfecter). The loaf and cup connect us with that kind of person, and then …
title: A Lesson from the Cross

content:
Coming here means giving credit where credit is due. Several TV commercials lately are making their appeals to “receive what you deserve.” Such wording does have a certain drawing power, but there is a more important idea that calls us not to take credit for what we have done and then appeal for what we deserve from doing it. As Jesus put it, we have only done our duty no matter how well we have done it (Luke 17:10).
Since our duty calls for perfection, there is no way to deserve some reward for …
title: Love Without Limits

content:
Jesus died on Friday, but we commemorate it on Sunday. That custom arose because his resurrection on the first day of the week made clear what his death on the cross meant three days earlier.
Two other men died that same day the same way, but Jesus was not a criminal executed for his own crimes, but a sacrifice offered for our sins. God made that clear by bringing him out of the tomb. This bread and grape juice stand for his body and blood, given and shed. As we say so often from the apostle …
title: Commemorated on Sunday

content:
These communion elements take us back to the hardest situation our Lord faced. Jesus could have prayed to the Father to send as many as 72,000 angels to protect him from this ordeal (Matthew 26:53). Instead, the Father sent him one angel to empower him with influence to deal with it (Luke 22:43).
God may not protect us either from the ordeals we face; but remembering our “older brother” here and the presence of the Spirit that’s always with us, is sufficient to empower us for times like that. …
title: One Angel of Encouragement

content:
A word particularly to you fathers today: Be struck by what you’re about to do.
I have two sons, David and Steve. We have worked together, played together, performed music together, talked a lot about lots of things, eaten countless meals across the table from each other for years. I can’t imagine being responsible for having David or Steve die a terrible death. I cannot imagine what it would take to bring myself to ask them to do that.
It’s no wonder Paul says, “A good man might die for a good …
title: Father’s Day

content:
“He is our Peace” (Ephesians 2:14). Paul writes that comment in reference to overcoming the Jew-Gentile enmity. He is referring to the wall in the Jews’ temple complex that divided the Court of the Gentiles from the rest of the worship center. So to speak, Christ tore down that separator and that separation.
The need for peace applies to a wide range of divisions ancient and modern. Christ no longer moves among us bodily, but he has left the church to be the “body of Christ” in the world …
title: Peace Through the Cross

content:
“Actions speak louder than words.” Jesus meant something like that when he said, “Nobody has greater love than to lay down his life for his friends” (John 15:13). He said that the night before he did that. His follow-up in the morning spoke more than all his sermons combined.
That same crucifixion eve, he instituted this simple custom to keep in remembrance of him and his life’s main principle. It won’t take us long this morning to repeat the custom, but it will take us all day and the rest of …
title: Do Something

content:
“Shedding blood” means dying an unnatural death, in this case a death for sins. Jesus maintained his mission till his dying breath. That was not just for a cause but to a person, the Father. Giving one’s life is the most anyone can do for any reason. Christ’s ultimate self-giving was also his last, coming as it did after a full life of righteous endeavor for God.
We identify with that righteousness when we join this observance. We commit to his values and purposes because he is Lord after …
title: Counted Righteous

content:
Ultimate issues call for ultimate measures, The ultimate issue everywhere has always been broken friendships, human and divine. That friendship consists of behaviors toward each other, not just closeness to, descent from, and likeness to.
If those behaviors and their attitudes and motives are self-centered, the associations are strained and broken. We call them “sins.”
So what happens now? This “breaking bread” calls for our undivided attention to what has happened: God has sent his Son to …
title: Discerning Christ’s Body

content:
Isaiah looked forward to see what we are looking back to remember: the suffering of Another because of what we have done. Were it not for our failures, there would have been no need for him to be saddened, misunderstood, despised, rejected, and abused to death.
Isaiah meant more than that our actions cause other people grief and pain. He meant more than that we’re the ones who deserve what they suffer. He meant more than that we cannot disentangle ourselves from the consequences of our own deeds …
title: Isaiah 53:2-12

content:
Life mixes sadness and joy. The one tempers the other, so happiness is not constant and sadness is not permanent. We may do well then to speak of joy since happiness depends on what “happens.” But joy overrides what’s happening and follows the hard knocks that come. Furthermore, anticipating joy strengthens present endurance, “For the joy that was set before him, Jesus endured the cross” (Hebrews 12:2).
Observing the bread and wine illustrates the point and affirms our convictions about it. On …
title: Joy in the Morning

content:
We are meeting at the table, not to remember a dead founder but to acknowledge a living Lord. Were it not for what astounded us at dawn, we would have no reason to be here much less to take up these markers of a death last Friday.
“Dead Messiah” would be a contradiction of terms because “Messiah abides forever” (John 12:34). It is not an abiding like our Lord’s contemporaries expected. He would not live and rule forever on earth; he would abide forever by first dying and resurrecting to rule …
title: Easter

content:
This observance reminds us of what can happen when we do not conform to the world’s expectations. Death is the most extreme consequence that might happen, so we can use this occasion together to resolve not to waffle should something demanding present itself to us. Christ calls us to transform our values and purposes, attitudes and motives, from what characterizes a world governed by materialistic, humanistic thinking.
For the most part, we face lesser consequences, things like exclusion from …
title: Transformation

content:
“I didn’t come to do my own will; I came to do my Father’s will.” The Father and the Son have a oneness in the sense of unity; they were at one—united in purpose to do what happened through Jesus’ ministry, including Gethsemane through Golgotha: “Not my will but yours be done” (Luke 22:42; Mark 14:36; Matthew 26:39, 42).
Taking these representations of his body and blood says to the Father that we too qualify our will by his. As Christ accepted his cross to show his obedience to the Father and …
title: John 6:38

content:
Nothing important is ever easy. It may be easy to understand, but doing it is another matter. The loaf and cup here in front of us remind us about the powerful temptation in the Garden, the temptation for Jesus to do other than what he knew was the Father’s will. They remind us that nothing is ever changed by staying in the Garden, never changed by knowing what to do. It takes coming out of the Garden, so to speak, to do what it takes.
Here we transfer the format to ourselves. Christ has called …
title: Carrying Crosses

content:
“To the One that can present you faultless with great joy before the only God our Savior, be glory . . . forevermore.” On that Great Day we don’t have to feel like he is looking at us with our accumulated past sins and mistakes in mind. He will be looking at us as we are then, which grows out of the message in these emblems.
Here is something of how it works. When I was about twelve, I missed the curve in our driveway and drove our 1946 Ford Fergusen tractor over an iron post near the lane. The …
title: Jude 24-25

content: Coming to the table connects us with the one event that reaches out in all directions in time and territory—present, past, and future; here, there, and everywhere. Christ’s culminating act of his ministry laid the basis for all salvation—under the Mosaic covenant (Hebrews 9:15), during the patriarchal age (1 Peter 4:6; 3:18-21), and henceforth to the Lord’s return (Matthew 28:18-20). He made possible the restored friendship with God and all people irrespective of race or status (Galatians 3:28). …
title: The Universal Solvent for Sin

content: “[Christ] is our peace, who united [Jews and Gentiles] and tore down the wall [between the court of Gentiles and the Jewish quarters in the temple at Jerusalem]. He abolished in his flesh [the source of] enmity between them, that is, the Law made up of commandments as ordinances. He did it to create in himself from the two a new united humankind, so making peace. He did it to reconcile them both in one body to God through the cross, having slain the enmity that way.” By being the One that all …
title: Ephesians 2:14-16

content: There is more than one way to mess up when we are dealing with people. We can be unaware that what we have done is harmful or offensive. We can fail to do what we know we should but forget to take care of it or not consider it important enough to worry about. In selfish moments, we know better but don’t care enough to restrain our impulses. We call them sins of ignorance, sins of omission, sins of commission. They are alike in their negative effects and our need to do what we can to reverse …
title: The Forgiveness Provision

content:
The Lord’s Supper pictures Jesus reversing the downward spiral of deteriorating relationships. On the cross he lived out in the extreme his own commandment to “turn the other cheek” (Matthew 5:39).
People usually respond in kind—good for good, bad for bad. The pattern leads to deepening discord. Stopping evil comes from not responding at all, by letting it die from lack of attention. Reversing the pattern comes from responding to evil with good.
Through Christ, God has demonstrated what it often …
title: New Year’s

content:
Each year offers a new beginning. On a smaller scale, each week at this table, these emblems remind us that the blood that saved us continues to cleanse us from sins (1 John 1:7). Those sins crop up as periodic failures to be what he has called us to be, shortcomings from what we have aspired to become.
That “cleansing” is not one and done, nor is it something that needs to be redone again and again. Rather, we experience ongoing relationship with the One who continues to forgive us as we …
title: New Year’s

content:
One act, so many things to learn from it.
We’ve known people that would not take an entry-level job and earn their way up to higher rank and better pay. They wanted to start high for top dollar. Why was that?
Whatever the reason, we recognize it as weakness. Jesus demonstrated what it means to have inner strength that is not tied to position and circumstance. He gave up being equal with God, became a man, and carried his humility to the point of “enduring the cross.” He prioritized accomplishing …
title: Philippians 2:5-8.

content:
Resisting temptation is as much a part of life as “doing the right thing.” Jesus did not call the more than 60,000 angels available to him to disperse the mob in Gethsemane (Matthew 26:23). He could “even now” ask the Father to send them, having already prayed earnestly three times to the Father not to let him get crucified.
He did not use any personal powers to drive his attackers away. John 18:6 does indicate that “they drew back and fell to the ground” when he confirmed that he was the One …
title: Symbols of Resistance

content:
“A friend loves at all times” (Proverbs 17:17), even when he is on a cross. In the Garden, Jesus protected his disciples from being caught up in the fray. After all, he was not leading an insurrection against the Jewish nation or Roman rule. This was his job alone, which had to do with an entirely different kind of “kingdom.”
He healed the severed ear of Malchus (John 18:10; Luke 22:51). Was Malchus a lead attacker as servant of the high priest there at Caiaphas’ behest? He was close enough to …
title: A Man for Others

content:
Truth is reality, and grace identifies the kind of reality Messiah brought for us to embody. “Law came by Moses, but grace and truth came by Jesus Messiah” (John 1:17). The point is not that the Law was false but that it was not the real thing; it drew a picture of the real thing, approximated it, prepared for its real expression in us: relationship to God and each other based on grace.
In the flesh-and-blood state (John 1:18), the Messiah expressed what we in the flesh and blood condition are …
title: The Real Thing

content: One notable feature of Christ’s crucifixion is that it was voluntary. Jesus himself did not try to fight against the arresting mob in Gethsemane. He did not use supernatural to drive the temple guard away-even though he evidently could have: the guard falling backward when he said, “I’m the one you are looking for”; let these others go” (John 18:10-11), He did not let his disciples—like Peter—fight in the Garden to defend him (John 18:10-11). Jesus pointed out to Pilate. “My kingdom is not of …
title: Voluntary Self-Sacrifice

content:
Rejection by the masses, ridicule by religious leaders, abandonment by disciples, and suffering from the Romans combined in the culminating event of the Messiah’s earthly life. He made it through that horrible experience by appealing to resources outside himself: the angel that “ministered to him” in the Garden, prayer to the Father, commitment to the purpose inside of “your will, not mine” and looking to the future joy beyond the present pain.
None of these resources were supernatural miracles …
title: Natural Ways to Cope

content:
The loaf and cup represent reasons for looking forward to the final proof of our faith. Our Lord’s vicious death sets up the fact of his victorious resurrection over death and over the ones that did it to him.
Jesus did not die from age, sickness, starvation, some accident, or a capital crime. He “shed his blood,” which means he died in an unnatural way. He did not just bleed from a cut; he bled to death from crucifixion. The wonderful thing about this horrible thing is that it gives us the …
title: Easter the Confidence Builder

content:
Getting something rolling is not the end of any work. Continued efforts must keep the matter rolling. Jesus’ ministry, his death and resurrection, and the “shedding forth” of the Spirit on Pentecost were not the end of the story. Luke summarizes the first Christians’ endeavors at carrying the faith forward right from the start: “They devoted themselves to the apostles’ teaching, fellowship, breaking bread, and prayers” (Acts 2:42).
Our gathering today incorporates these same four observances, …
title: A Week after Pentecost Sunday

content:
We always stand at the junction between past and future. That means we benefit from both God’s deeds from the past and his promises about the future. The things he has done guarantee the things he has said he’ll do.
As that present junction point moves forward, we carry with us observances that combine memory and hope. The Lord’s Supper is one such observance. That fact appears in one of Paul’s comments to the Corinthians: “As often as you eat this bread and drink this cup you show the Lord’s …
title: 1 Corinthians 11:26

content:
Observing the Lord’s Supper supplies a corrective on church life. In one of the most familiar passages on this matter, Paul says,
“I received from the Lord what I passed on to you. The night he was betrayed he took a loaf, gave thanks, broke it, and said, ‘This is my body, which is for you. Do this in memory of me.’ After the meal he took the cup, ‘This cup is the New Covenant in my blood. As often as you drink it, do it in memory of me.’”
The body and blood that he gave is a correction on the …
title: 1 Corinthians 11:23-25

content:
Do you ever wonder whether somebody loves you? Do your parents care about you? What about your children? Do you think your husband, your wife, still loves you? What do your friends say that makes you confident that they care? Do your neighbors and fellow workers and church members do things that let you know how they regard you? Does it cross your mind that they may not mean it?
When it comes to the Lord’s Supper, we get a gratifying answer to this deep-down question that everybody asks. Nobody, …
title: Tokens of Love

content: “You [Gentiles] were separated from Christ . . ., separated from the commonwealth of Israel, without hope and without God in the world. But you that were once afar off have come near by the blood of Christ. He’s the basis for peace between us. He made both of us into one group, tore down the dividing barrier between us, and abolished in his flesh the law made up of commanded regulations. That way, from the two groups he could create in himself one new united mankind, making peace between us, and …
title: Ephesians 2:11-16a

content:
We do not serve a dead Savior; we serve a living Lord. So the emblems he instituted for remembering his broken body and shed blood picture obedience to him as resurrected Lord. The reason there are emblems of his body and blood is that’s what he gave in obedience to the Father.
Likewise, our resurrected Lord ever lives to receive our total, permanent, and exclusive obedience. And he ever lives to intercede for us because our obedience is not always complete.
The overarching fact here is that we …
title: Emblems of Obedience

content:
The bread and fruit of the vine are more than what they picture. They represent something that leads to what comes back on us to empower us for whatever lies between now and the coming joy. We can run steadfastly the race that is set before us because we are looking here to “Jesus the author and perfecter of our faith” (Hebrews 12:2a). “For the joy that was set before him at the right hand of the Father, he endured the cross and disregarded the shame” (12:2b).
We who wear his name likewise deal …
title: Resurrection

content:
The night Jesus instituted the Lord’s Supper, he told his disciples that he would not be drinking the fruit of the vine with them again till the kingdom of God had come (Matthew 26:29; Mark 14:25; Luke 22:15, 18). This would be the last Passover meal he would observe with them; the shedding of his blood and the giving of his body would happen the next morning. For our purposes today, the point is that he would drink it with his disciples when the kingdom had come.
As surely as he ate three days …
title: Jesus Beside Us

content:
Early in Jesus’ ministry, he told the disciples he had go to Jerusalem and suffer a lot of things from the religious leaders and even be killed. That cloud hung over his entire ministry, but it was something he had to do, so he did it.
When we “come to the table,” we look back at his death and acknowledge the principle of fulfilling what is ours to do before God and other people. That is especially important when it comes to matters that only we are in a position to handle. Maybe it’s just that …
title: Matthew 16:21-22

content:
God has given us a wide range of freedom in which to use our power of choice. We live within a broad arrow of options. As long as our choices fall within the limits of that arrow, we are moving along toward the Lord’s intended destiny for us. The garden in Genesis 2 pictures our circumstance before our Creator. Adam and Eve could eat the fruit from countless trees; they were to leave just one of them alone.
We are looking forward to a new year of making a living and enjoying other activities. …
title: New Year’s

content:
Family is a big part of this season. We take off work to spend time with family. We travel to be with family—sometimes across the state, across the country, even across the ocean. We may get together several times during these holidays. We exchange gifts and just sit around and talk or play games or go hunting. Lots of food gets prepared and enjoyed—all in the family setting. It is bonding time.
The coming of Messiah was in a family, not in a solitary public demonstration. This feature of his …
title: Christmas and Family

content:
Even Satan understands us well enough to know that we will give everything we own to preserve our life (Job 2:4). That is how valuable we consider life. We would have to think something is awfully important before we’d voluntarily give up our life for it.
In that light, we gather around these two emblems just now. They draw us back to the giving of a man’s life, and not to just any life—the most important life ever—the life of the Lord himself. This occasion reminds us how much we are worth, how …
title: A Precious Life

content:
When our Lord instituted this observance, he said, “This is my body that is given for you”; this is my blood that is given for you” (1 Corinthians 11:24, etc.). No one took it from him; he gave it willingly (John 10:18). And it did not just happen; he did it deliberately for a reason—for us.
This most notable feature of the Messiah’s coming is still reflected in the secular Christmas season, even among people who are not in close connection with the meaning of the celebration. They give …
title: Christmas

content:
Funny how little things stick with you. When I was in the third grade, a photographer came to our school and took pictures of us. When the individual billfold-size shots came, on the little package in blue letters, I remember seeing, “A picture is worth a thousand words.” That was my first exposure to the well-known expression.
Today we say these emblems “speak to us”; they’re “worth a thousand words.” They’re a visual message that brings back what took place real-ly so long ago. Grape juice and …
title: A Thousand Words

content:
Several kinds of things make us thankful. We are grateful that we were not frustrated in what we wanted to accomplish—it did not rain before we could get the hay in the barn.
We are grateful that we had help doing what we could not do by ourselves—as when people helped us move the piano in from the U-Haul and take it upstairs.
We are grateful for something nice that came unexpectedly out of someone’s good will—and the thoughtful motorist who stopped and changed the tire that our own tire tools …
title: Thanksgiving: What We Are Grateful For

content:
Most of our time we spend on smaller things: getting the shopping done, mowing the lawn, watching a baseball game.
Much of what we use our abilities for are not the most important matters we face: learning to play an instrument in the high school band that we might not find much use for after we graduate, learning to play basketball although we will not likely be skilled enough to make a living at it later.
A good bit of what we spend our money on will not be a permanent solution to anything: …
title: What Matters Most

content:
Reversing a trend is hard to do but necessary to be done. Our behavior brings consequences that form a series; that series tends to get worse and spread to other things, and we end up with a cumulative effect we don’t want but can’t stop.
Christ’s mission had to reverse a pattern we’ve all caught ourselves up in. That was harder for him to do than for us to get it started. His work aimed at stopping what had been in progress since God created our first parents. Jesus did more than teach about …
title: Reversing the Trend

content:
“He has borne our griefs and carried our sorrows; yet we considered him struck by God and afflicted. But he was wounded because of our transgressions and bruised because of our sins. The chastisement to bring us peace was laid on him, and by his stripes we are healed. We have all gone astray like sheep and turned to our own way. The Lord has laid on him the iniquity of us all.”
Often the things we do cause us to suffer. More than that, they often cause other people to suffer. And the worst part …
title: Isaiah 53:4-6

content:
“If we have participated in what is like [Christ’s] death, we will participate in what is like his resurrection.”
In our baptism we said we were “burying” the old way of living and “resurrecting” to a new one. That act looked forward to renewed fellowship with God through a new identity with his Son. Friendship with God is not the kind of thing that can be finished business The meaning of breaking bread together corresponds with the meaning of our original commitment. It acknowledges our ongoing …
title: Romans 6:5

content:
“I am not alone because the Father is with me.”
A genuine leader must be willing to stand alone when necessary. That feature played out in the extreme in Christ’s bringing in the “kingdom” of God. As the distinctives of his work drew toward their conclusion, he found himself alone. His own disciples scattered when the Shepherd was struck, and they did so despite their resolve “even to die with him” (Matthew 26:35).
From time to time, we find ourselves in the minority side, or even more …
title: John 16:32b

content:
“Do you love me more than these do?” What do you do when you know that “sticking to your guns” will cost you dearly? You will not get hired for a job you need and want. You will get passed over for a promotion, you will get fired, get fined, get jailed, get shunned by friends, disowned by parents, divorced by your spouse! What do you do? So to speak, you take communion.
As long as loving Christ does not conflict with loving certain things and certain ones, all is well. Who you are and what you …
title: John 21:18

content:
The Father has made peace through blood shed on a cross. That peace consists of reconciliation, which reverses alienation (Colossians 1:19-20). Peace between people makes peace possible between nations and with other kinds of hostilities. Peace between people also creates the circumstance for peace within us. Feeling accepted and forgiven removes the inner conflict between what we aspire to be and what we achieve in living.
Taking communion brings back the memories of what it took to lay the …
title: Let There Be Peace

content:
Some things only certain people can do; they are the only ones with the knowledge required. We go to a doctor to get help with medical problems because we do not have the expertise ourselves to cope with those issues. Most people we know are limited in how much they can help with health concerns. We need a specialist to diagnose and treat our life-threating concerns.
Some things only certain people can do; they are the only ones with the abilities required. If the team needs a point guard, they …
title: The Only One That Can

content:
We want to get close so we can understand. Being present at what’s happening gives us a better feel for it than hearing someone’s report or seeing it on television.
As to convictions, we believe that God knows and understands our human situation, but in our sense of things we long for “Immanuel.” Among several things, God’s nearness helps us feel that he does, in fact, “understand our frame” (Psalm 103:14). Without thinking, we project onto him the limitation of our own viewpoint—knowing better …
title: Immanuel

content: To demonstrate divine power over human opposition, the Father could have removed “the cup” his Son would drink in six hours—but he didn’t. Jesus could have just walked away as he had on other occasions—but he didn’t (Luke 4:30; John 8:99; 10:39). He could have restrained the acts of his enemies, caused them to cower in apprehension (John 18:6) or walk away astounded at his powerful words (John 7:45)—but he didn’t (John 7:46; 18:6). He did not let his disciples fight for him (Matthew 26:51-52). …
title: Drinking the Cup

content:
What price, success! Things don’t just happen; they don’t just take care of themselves, and they don’t just do it quickly and easily, especially big things, important things. Success calls for a willingness to do whatever it takes in effort made and in risk taken—in loss, danger, suffering.
Christ had no personal home or immediate family. His work led to rejection by the religious establishment and growing threats against his very life. Finally, he felt the pain of thorns, scourging, and …
title: The Price of Success

content:
Nothing worth having is easy to get. We talk about hard work as requiring blood, sweat, and tears. Indeed, what price, change!
In laying the groundwork for that endeavor, Jesus prayed with “strong crying and tears” (Hebrews 5:7) to the One who could save him from crucifixion. Some copies of Luke note that in the Garden during that prayer he sweat, as it were, drops of blood (Luke 22:44). The crown of thorns, the scourgings, and the crucifixion shed his blood. Christ’s mission cost the sweat of …
title: The Price of Change

content:
Bucking popular viewpoints got our savior killed. He did not reinforce the opinions of political and religious heads of his day, nor did he confirm the expectations of the general public. He needed to withstand the misunderstandings and consequent bullying of the masses, or they would have had no reason to depart the ill-fated ramifications of their erroneous opinions.
As a growing concern in the modern world, we face this same age-old dynamic that tries to press religion into a foreign role. It …
title: Picking Up Crosses

content:
Free Indeed
The more important something is, the more it costs. “What price freedom!” In a concerted way we remember annually those who have given that “last measure of devotion” to secure and protect what we consider certain “inalienable rights”: life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness.
Gathering in this memorial observance, we acknowledge in a concerted way what it took to secure and protect the even more difficult aspect of human liberty—freedom from the power and penalty of personal sin. …
